title: The Duke Ellington and Count Basie joint album
summary: Jones tells how Columbia and Roulette teamed the two bands for one day, with Duke writing harsh clashes that left Basie's men soaked.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: You told me a story one day off the tape when we were sitting here, about -- I think it was when Duke and Basie were recording in New York and you were there.
Oh, yeah.
And tell me -- tell that story on the tape. I like that.

Let me see, I'm trying to find some high points to it. Okay. I'll give you a little background first. Roulette Records had recorded Louis Armstrong and Duke in Europe. Bob Thiele Field was instrumental, I think, in putting that together.
no in N.Y.
Uh-huh.
So Duke was on Columbia at that point, so Ellington was the big Columbia man, big band man, and Basie was the big Roulette man.
Uh-huh.

So to make it even the companies got together and had a handshake on it and said well, let's -- instead of just recording just Basie -- I think this was the way it went, I'm not sure -- just Basie on Columbia or something like it, let's record both of the bands, you know?
Uh-huh.

And they did the whole album in one day. They had been on the road, you know, just passing through, and Tom Whaley Wheeler, Duke's orchestrator, had a table off to the side, you know, and he was writing, and -- now this was basically Ellington's date, because it was with his company, you know, the company he was signed with. And Duke wrote some -- he used some of the things out of, I think, "Paris Blues,"
that was one thing that he used that Louis Armstrong played in the picture.
Uh-huh.

And I'll never forget the way the Basie Band looked, because at that time they had Marshall Royal (PHONETIC), Budd Johnson. They had a -- you know, it was two great bands. But Duke had written so many -- you know, he wrote very like clashes, notes rubbing together.
That's an interesting description.
Yeah, you know?
Uh-huh.
And when they finished doing this thing with Louis, that thing they did in, 'Paris Blues,' some of the Basie guys were soaking wet. L (Battle Royal)
(Laughter)
So Marshall Royal told me, he said, 'The old man is really splitting atoms on that one.'
(Laughter)

You know? And how they made -- but Duke was so smart in that -- I think Teo Macero (PHONETIC) was in the booth, you know, the producer, and they wanted to make it like a battle of jazz, but Duke didn't have it that way. When Thad Jones would take a solo, Duke would have his reed section play behind him. And when Ray Nance would play a solo, Duke would have Basie's reed section play behind him. So it was like all
one whole complete thing. And I think -- what Duke was really thinking about, he wasn't thinking about a comparison. He said, "Gee, I've got 10 great saxophone players."
Sure he was.

Two great drummers, two fine bass players, you know, and he just wished he had more time to do it, you know? But when he did it, had everybody -- oh, yeah, they were just -- a couple of guys almost started a fight, but they cooled it out, you know.
